content: Hip dysplasia, also known as developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) or congenital dysplasia of the hip (CDH), refers to a condition where the hip joint is either malformed or misaligned. This can be present at birth or develop later in life. The term developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) is often preferred over congenital dislocation of the hip (CDH) because the latter is considered less flexible in describing the range of potential complications. The term congenital implies that the condition is present at birth, but this can be misleading since the hip joint in newborns is primarily composed of cartilage and remains malleable, making it difficult to determine the exact onset of the condition. For example, a hip joint may be underdeveloped without dislocation at birth, with dislocation occurring later. The terminology is inconsistently applied, with pediatric and neonatal orthopedics using it to describe unstable or poorly developed hips, while in adults, it refers to hips with abnormal femoral head or acetabular structures visible on X-rays. Some experts prefer the term hip dysplasia for its simplicity and accuracy, avoiding redundancy in the phrase developmental dysplasia. Hip dysplasia can vary in severity, from subtle abnormalities to severe malformations or dislocations. The congenital form, known as teratologic or non-reducible dislocation, is often associated with more complex conditions. The condition can affect one or both hips. Bilateral dysplasia involves both hip joints, making diagnostic indicators like asymmetric folds or leg-length discrepancies less applicable. In unilateral dysplasia, only one hip joint is affected, and the contralateral side may show compensatory changes. Most unilateral cases involve the left hip. In cases of complete dislocation, a false acetabulum may form higher on the pelvis opposite the dislocated femoral head. Acetabular dysplasia occurs when the acetabulum (hip socket) is too shallow or deformed. The center-edge angle, as described by Wiberg, is used to measure this. In coxa vara, the femoral head grows at an excessively narrow angle to the femoral shaft, while in coxa valga, the angle is too wide. A rare form, Beukes familial hip dysplasia, is found among Afrikaners of the Beukes family and is characterized by a flat, irregular femoral head, leading to early-onset osteoarthritis. In 1979, Dr. John F. Crowe and colleagues proposed a classification system to define the degree of hip malformation and dislocation, ranging from the least severe (Crowe I) to the most severe (Crowe IV). This classification is particularly useful for evaluating treatment outcomes. Instead of relying on the Wiberg angle, which is less effective for quantifying dislocation, they used three key elements: a reference line at the lower rim of the teardrop feature on X-rays, the junction between the femoral head and neck, and the height of the pelvis. By analyzing anteroposterior pelvic X-rays, they measured the degree of femoral head subluxation. A normal femoral head diameter is approximately 20% of the pelvic height. If the femoral head-neck junction is more than 10% of the pelvic height above the reference line, the joint is considered more than 50% dislocated. Determining the incidence of hip dysplasia is challenging because many cases resolve spontaneously. An instability rate of 1 in 60 has been reported, which decreases to 1 in 240 by one week of age. The condition is more common in females than males. Hip dysplasia is considered a multifactorial condition, meaning multiple factors contribute to its development. Congenital causes may include hormonal influences, such as the hormone relaxin, which has been implicated in some studies. Genetic factors also play a role, with specific loci identified on chromosomes 13 and 4q35. Beukes familial dysplasia maps to an 11-cM region on chromosome 4q35, with nonpenetrant carriers unaffected. Acquired hip dysplasia has been linked to cultural practices like swaddling or the use of cradleboards, which restrict hip movement in an abducted position for extended periods. Modern swaddling techniques allow for more leg movement. Other risk factors include breech birth and being a firstborn child. In breech positions, the femoral head is more likely to be displaced from the socket. A narrow uterus can also contribute to hip joint dislocation during fetal development and birth. Most countries include hip joint screening in standard newborn exams to detect hip dysplasia early. The condition can often be identified by a click or clunk in the hip, although not all clicks indicate dysplasia. The Ortolani and Barlow maneuvers are commonly used in neonatal exams for diagnosis. Confirmation can be achieved through ultrasound and X-rays. Ultrasound is particularly effective in defining hip anatomy before cartilage ossifies. By around three months of age, clear radiographic images can be obtained. However, this is also the point at which nonsurgical treatment methods become less effective. On X-rays, dislocation may be indicated if Shenton's line, an arc drawn from the medial femoral neck through the superior margin of the obturator foramen, is disrupted. Asymmetrical gluteal folds and apparent limb-length discrepancies can also indicate unilateral hip dysplasia. Ligamentous laxity in newborn hips and stable appearances in severely malformed joints highlight the importance of follow-up exams and developmental monitoring. Routine ultrasound screening has been debated and rejected due to the small benefit not justifying the cost. The Harris hip score, developed by Dr. William H. Harris, is one method for evaluating hip function after surgery, alongside other scoring systems like the Oxford hip score, HOOS, and WOMAC. The Children's Hospital Oakland Hip Evaluation Scale (CHOHES) is a modified version of the Harris hip score currently under evaluation. Treatment of hip dysplasia aims to prevent long-term complications such as limping, chronic pain, and impaired mobility. Early intervention and developmental monitoring are crucial. In infants, early hip dysplasia can often be treated with a Pavlik harness or Frejka pillow/splint during the first year of life, usually with good outcomes. However, cases of femoral head avascular necrosis have been reported with the Pavlik harness, though it remains unclear whether these are due to improper application or complications of the disorder itself. Other devices, such as spica casts, are used, particularly after surgical closed reduction. Traction may also be employed as part of the treatment plan. In older children, surgical intervention may be necessary to address contractures in the hip abductor and iliopsoas muscles, which adapt to the dislocated joint position. Braces and splints are often used post-surgery to continue treatment. While some children outgrow untreated mild hip dysplasia with little or no impact on quality of life, studies have not yet identified reliable methods for predicting outcomes. Delayed treatment, however, is associated with complications and poor results. Research into stem cell therapies is ongoing, including bone grafting and seeding porous arthroplasty prostheses with autologous fibroblasts or chondrocyte progenitor cells to improve anchoring of artificial materials in the bone bed. Hip dysplasia is a common cause of early-onset osteoarthritis of the hip due to abnormal load-bearing surfaces, which lead to increased and uneven wear. Total hip arthroplasty (hip replacement) is often required but can be complicated by the need for revision surgery due to skeletal changes, loosening, wear, or bone resorption. Osteotomies may be performed alone or in conjunction with arthroplasty to correct misalignment.
